verified: The packet's 'existing approved text' (RU/EN) matches the bundle exactly. The claim is domain material_culture, supported_fact, editorial/medium, applicability 1200–1300 region_novgorod_land, hard_exclusion null. edits_vs_packet_and_why: 'В мире' / 'in this world' -> 'в Новгородской земле' / 'in the Novgorod Land'. This matches the claim's place applicability (region_novgorod_land). The unscoped wording can be read as a global historical statement, which is false: gunpowder was known in China and used in Jin–Mongol warfare around 1232. It can also be read as a statement about physical possibility, which D59 forbids.
Restored 'для боя' / 'for battle' to keep the text faithful to the canonical object literal and to the evidence scope (gunpowder in battle). Dropping it widened the statement beyond its evidence.

Accepted the removal of the sentence 'Воюют мечом, копьём, луком да самострелом' / 'War is fought with…'. It is not part of the exclusion and the editorial evidence note does not cover it. Removing it adds nothing false.

tanning.note: The packet underuses its own source. ¶1836 (Kolchin, ch. 'Ремесло') directly attests many Novgorod tanners' workshops of the XI–XIV c. (large ash-lime deposits mixed with hair; liming vats made as log troughs or thick-stave tubs). ¶1834 gives the Rus process with bark tanning. This would close the gap verification-hide-processing.md left open ('a separate historical source is required for any 1100–1300 Novgorod compatibility claim'). Recommended as a separate historical claim in a later wave; not required here.

birch_tar.checked: Both claim:place-thermal-birch-tar-* claims are craft_technology supported_fact, 1200–1300 Novgorod Land, inferred/medium, from source:place-thermal-birch-tar-schmidt-2023 ('Production method of the Königsaue birch tar documents cumulative culture in Neanderthals'). They state only a heating/collection relation and oxygen/collection conditions. book:804890 ¶136 contains «перегонялось на огне без доступа воздуха» verbatim (late ethnography). The limits are correct.
birch_tar.note: The packet missed two things. (a) The existing claim:household-tar-pot (ceramic pots with tar in an excavation; 1100–1300 Novgorod, inferred). (b) book:622242 ¶848 (Kuza), which lists 'производство дегтя' among Old Rus peasant trades. Both are broad historical context, not Novgorod-specific birch-tar production, method, installation or yield. The packet's 'do not strengthen local production' still holds. A broad Old Rus historical_availability claim from ¶848 could be drafted later.

iron.checked: The smithing-scope claims are correctly scoped: claim:occupation-smith-iron-input (smithing requires_input iron; 'iron was supplied by rural metallurgists; the urban smithy worked already obtained metal'; 1100–1300, inferred/medium); occupation-smith-anvil/hammer/tongs (attested_use); claim:reconstructed-place-work-smithy-… (editorial work context); claim:ordinary-life-smith-needs-iron-and-fuel; the universal static-forge-welding-* claims. book:622242 ¶1559 contains «мелко раздробленную железную руду с большим количеством древесного угля» verbatim. The ¶¶1559–1584 and ¶¶1597–1605 descriptions in the packet are accurate; the cited smithy and anvils are mostly outside Novgorod, and one anvil is from early XIV c. Novgorod.
iron.correction: The packet's limit says this source 'does not establish … Novgorod primary smelting'. That is too coarse. Use instead: ¶1584 directly attests commodity blooms in Novgorod layers of the XIII–early XIV c. (rough semi-products that smiths had to forge further). ¶1555 says Rus iron was produced by village metallurgists, separate from smithing. The existing approved claim:occupation-smith-iron-input already gives rural metallurgists supplying Novgorod (inferred/medium). What stays unproven: specific smelting sites, bog-ore deposits or furnaces in Novgorod Land (the sites in ¶1562 are outside it), stock, charge, yield, duration and a finished knife.

5_bloomery_drafting.rationale: Under D59, a player's attempt to make iron from real inputs is judged causally, so the A1 owner needs atomic causal premises. book:622242 ¶¶1555–1585 (Kolchin, ch. 'Ремесло') is a solid scholarly source. Ore reduction is not smithing and must not be put under wk:craft_technology:smithing. universal_claims.subject: wk:physics_material_science:iron-oxide-reduction
universal_claims.proposition: In a charcoal-fired column, hot carbon monoxide from burning charcoal can reduce iron oxide in ore to solid metallic iron grains without melting the iron.

universal_claims.subject: wk:physics_material_science:iron-oxide-reduction
universal_claims.proposition: Separating the ore's waste rock as liquid slag needs a substantially higher temperature throughout the furnace than reduction alone; if it is too low, the reduced iron grains stay trapped in unmelted rock.

universal_claims.subject: wk:physics_material_science:iron-oxide-reduction
universal_claims.proposition: Reaching and holding those temperatures through a column of ore and charcoal depends on continuous forced air supply.

universal_claims.subject: wk:physics_material_science:iron-oxide-reduction
universal_claims.proposition: The reduced grains collect low in the furnace and weld into a porous spongy mass (bloom) still impregnated with slag; slag is a separate by-product.

universal_claims.subject: wk:material_culture:iron-ore
universal_claims.proposition: Because slagging the waste rock consumes iron oxide, this process needs iron-rich ore; lean ore loses much of its iron to slag.

universal_claims.subject: wk:material_culture:iron-bloom
universal_claims.proposition: A raw bloom is not yet solid workable metal; it must be compressed while still hot to expel slag and weld it into one piece.
universal_claims.note: Reuse the existing static-forge-welding-* claims for the heat-plus-pressure joining physics; do not duplicate them.

historical_claims.applicability: Old Rus; Novgorod Land inferred/medium; must stay consistent with claim:occupation-smith-iron-input; no site in Novgorod Land asserted

historical_claims.subject: wk:material_culture:iron-bloom
historical_claims.proposition: Commodity blooms, rough spongy semi-products forged further by town and village smiths, are attested in Novgorod layers of the XIII–early XIV c.
historical_claims.note: The typical flat round form of about 3–6 kg (¶1582) may go only into the evidence note as non-binding context.

historical_claims.subject: wk:craft_technology:bloom-consolidation
historical_claims.proposition: Right after smelting, while still hot, the bloom was compressed with large wooden mallets or a stone-faced hammer on a wooden block or flat stone.

historical_claims.proposition: Town smiths further forged commodity blooms into dense, slag-poor iron before making objects.
historical_claims.note: This is a smithing input and is allowed on smithing. Ore reduction is not.

historical_claims.subject: wk:craft_technology:bloomery-iron-smelting
historical_claims.proposition: Rus metallurgists enriched ore before smelting by drying (weathering), roasting, crushing and winnowing.

No durations (the source gives none; time owner unchanged). No charge ratio, quantity, yield or success rate.

Temperatures (¶1573, ¶1602) and furnace, tuyere and bloom dimensions (¶¶1572, 1576, 1582) are not mechanics. They may appear only in evidence notes as non-binding context, not in canonical objects or runtime text.
No local ore deposit, smelting site, furnace, bellows, charcoal stock or metallurgist in any scene. No actor knowledge or skill. No finished item (knife, tool).
